Concrete is hard but brittle

It's not that. Concrete isn't that hard and it's not technically brittle in compression (it can take up to a 50% extra deformation from it's point of max stress, from ~2/1000 to ~3/1000 )

Concrete's problem is that it's very weak in tension, with resistances of around 5% to 10% it's compressive capacity (normally hydraulic and/or plastic shrinkage are enough to crack the zones in tenision).

That's why concrete nees reinforcement.

Prestressed and post-tensioned concrete is an interesting step forward from plain reinforced. Putting the tension zones in compression before the load is applied opens up a whole range of possibilities. Parking garages for one are a perfect representation of the possible applications

One of the things that dissapointed me when I took my first course on pre(post)-stressed concrete was that the resistance of a normal reinforced concrete member with the same amount of steel is very close to the pre(post)-stressed member (if I recall correctly, it's like 90% for members with adhered cables and like 97~98% for members with non-adhered cables).

The real difference is in stifness, pre(post)-stressed members deflect much less than regular members, especially in long term deformation (creep). That's why they are so used in parking lots, bridges and open plan buildings, they allow for much longer spans for the same section depth.
